Based on the healthcare Q&A matches provided, it appears that specialty care, particularly cardiologist care, is associated with improved survival rates in patients with congestive heart failure (CHF). A mixture of general practitioner and cardiologist care compared to general practitioner care showed an improved survival outcome. Additionally, the study suggests that outpatient care may be important for patient survival.

In contrast, distance to provider was not found to be a significant barrier to care for Medicaid patients with breast, colorectal, or lung cancer in general, although it may be relevant in certain situations due to travel burden associated with timely diagnosis and treatment. However, the study did find that self-reported health-related quality of life provides independent prognostic information for survival in non-small-cell lung cancer patients.

Regarding pulmonic valve replacement in adults late after repair of tetralogy of Fallot, the study suggests that performing the procedure before right ventricular recovery may be compromised in the adult population. This highlights the importance of considering pulmonary valve implantation before RV function deteriorates.

Finally, tumor expression of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) was not found to be associated with venous invasion and survival in patients with pT3 renal cell carcinoma, although VEGF is an independent prognostic factor in poor prognosis tumors.
